claim: In eukaryotic cells, intracellular components are organized by the microtubule motors cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) and kinesins.
source: In eukaryotic cells, intracellular components are organized by the microtubule motors cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) and kinesins, which are linked to cargos via adaptor proteins.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cellular organization and motor proteins.

claim: Approximately 40 kinesins transport cargo toward the plus end of microtubules.
source: While ~40 kinesins transport cargo toward the plus end of microtubules, a single dynein moves cargo in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about the number and function of kinesin motors.

claim: A single dynein moves cargo toward the minus end of microtubules.
source: While ~40 kinesins transport cargo toward the plus end of microtubules, a single dynein moves cargo in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about dynein function.

claim: Human cells have three Hooks (Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3).
source: Human cells have one FTS, three Hooks (Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3), and four FHIPs (FHIP1A, FHIP1B, FHIP2A, and FHIP2B) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1B showing three Hook proteins in H. sapiens.

claim: Human cells have four FHIPs (FHIP1A, FHIP1B, FHIP2A, and FHIP2B).
source: Human cells have one FTS, three Hooks (Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3), and four FHIPs (FHIP1A, FHIP1B, FHIP2A, and FHIP2B) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1B showing four FHIP proteins in H. sapiens.

claim: Human cells have one FTS protein.
source: Human cells have one FTS, three Hooks (Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3), and four FHIPs (FHIP1A, FHIP1B, FHIP2A, and FHIP2B) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1B showing one FTS protein in H. sapiens.

claim: Hook1 and Hook3 are present in the FHIP1A and FHIP1B BioID datasets.
source: Only Hook1 and Hook3 are present in the FHIP1A and FHIP1B BioID datasets, while all three Hooks are present in the FHIP2A and FHIP2B datasets (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the BioID data shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: All three Hooks are present in the FHIP2A and FHIP2B BioID datasets.
source: Only Hook1 and Hook3 are present in the FHIP1A and FHIP1B BioID datasets, while all three Hooks are present in the FHIP2A and FHIP2B datasets (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the BioID data shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: FHIP2A and FHIP2B are present in the Hook2 BioID dataset.
source: We performed a similar BioID experiment for Hook2 and found only FHIP2A and FHIP2B in the Hook2 BioID dataset (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the BioID data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP1A and FHIP1B coimmunoprecipitated Hook1 and Hook3, but not Hook2.
source: Supporting this, 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP1A and FHIP1B expressed in 293T cells coimmunoprecipitated Hook1 and Hook3, but not Hook2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hook1 and Hook3 coimmunoprecipitated FHIP1B.
source: In the converse experiment, Hook1 and Hook3 coimmunoprecipitated FHIP1B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP2A coimmunoprecipitated Hook2 and Hook3, with FHIP2A coimmunoprecipitating Hook2 to a much greater extent than Hook3.
source: 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP2A coimmunoprecipitated Hook2 and Hook3, with FHIP2A coimmunoprecipitating Hook2 to a much greater extent than Hook3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hook2 coimmunoprecipitated FHIP2A.
source: In the converse experiment, Hook2 coimmunoprecipitated FHIP2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP2B coimmunoprecipitated Hook2 and Hook3.
source: Though 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP2B only coimmunoprecipitated Hook2 and Hook3 (Figure 2B), all three Hook proteins coimmunoprecipitated FHIP2B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All three Hook proteins coimmunoprecipitated FHIP2B.
source: Though 3XFLAG-tagged FHIP2B only coimmunoprecipitated Hook2 and Hook3 (Figure 2B), all three Hook proteins coimmunoprecipitated FHIP2B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Purified full-length Hook2 activates dynein/dynactin motility in vitro.
source: We performed in vitro motility assays with purified dynein labeled with Alexa-TMR, unlabeled dynactin and unlabeled full-length Hook2 in the presence of Lis1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lis1 increases the formation of activated dynein/dynactin complexes.
source: We included Lis1 since it increases the formation of activated dynein/dynactin complexes (Elshenawy et al., 2020; Htet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Elshenawy et al., 2020; Htet et al., 2020).

claim: Lis1 led to a ~threefold increase in the number of processive dynein/dynactin runs activated by full-length Hook2.
source: Doing so led to a ~threefold increase in the number of processive dynein/dynactin runs activated by full-length Hook2 (Figure 3B – top panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Dynein/dynactin complexes activated by full-length Hook2 or full-length Hook3 in the presence of Lis1 moved at similar speeds.
source: Dynein/dynactin complexes activated by full-length Hook2 or full-length Hook3 in the presence of Lis1 moved at similar speeds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Moving dynein/dynactin complexes associate with FTS, Hook2, and FHIP2A-Alexa 660 complexes.
source: Reconstitution of FTS, Hook2, and FHIP2A-Alexa 660, as well as FTS, Hook3, and FHIP1B-Alexa 660 complexes in the presence of TMR-labeled dynein and unlabeled dynactin (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) revealed the colocalization of TMR-dynein with FHIP2A-Alexa 660 (Figure 3B – bottom panel, yellow arrows; top panel – controls) and FHIP1B-660 (Figure 3C – bottom panel, yellow arrows; top panel – controls).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Moving dynein/dynactin complexes associate with FTS, Hook3, and FHIP1B-Alexa 660 complexes.
source: Reconstitution of FTS, Hook2, and FHIP2A-Alexa 660, as well as FTS, Hook3, and FHIP1B-Alexa 660 complexes in the presence of TMR-labeled dynein and unlabeled dynactin (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) revealed the colocalization of TMR-dynein with FHIP2A-Alexa 660 (Figure 3B – bottom panel, yellow arrows; top panel – controls) and FHIP1B-660 (Figure 3C – bottom panel, yellow arrows; top panel – controls).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No colocalization or motile events were observed when Hook2 or Hook3 were omitted from the reaction mixtures.
source: Consistent with the role of Hook proteins in both activating dynein/dynactin complexes and linking them to FHIP/FTS, we did not observe any colocalization or motile events when Hook2 or Hook3 were omitted from the reaction mixtures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The colocalization of FHF complexes with moving dynein/dynactin had no effect or only minimal effects on dynein's motile properties including velocity, landing rates, pausing frequencies, and number of processive runs.
source: The colocalization of these FHF complexes with moving dynein/dynactin had no effect or only minimal effects on dynein's motile properties including velocity, landing rates, pausing frequencies, and number of processive runs (Figure 3D-G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-H).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3D-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-H.

claim: Run lengths increased slightly for FTS, Hook2, FHIP2A complexes compared to complexes lacking FTS and FHIP2A.
source: Run lengths increased slightly for FTS, Hook2, FHIP2A complexes compared to complexes lacking FTS and FHIP2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: No difference in run lengths was detected for FTS, Hook3, FHIP1B complexes compared to those lacking FTS and FHIP1B.
source: No difference in run lengths was detected for FTS, Hook3, FHIP1B complexes compared to those lacking FTS and FHIP1B (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Replacement of FHIP2A with FHIP1B in the FTS/Hook2 mixture led to very rare nonmotile colocalization events.
source: Replacing FHIP2A with FHIP1B in the FTS/Hook2 mixture led to very rare nonmotile colocalization events (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Replacement of FHIP1B with FHIP2A in the FTS/Hook3 mixture led to very rare colocalization between motile TMR-dynein and FHIP2A-Alexa-660.
source: Replacement of FHIP1B with FHIP2A in the FTS/Hook3 mixture also led to very rare colocalization between motile TMR-dynein and FHIP2A-Alexa-660 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule motility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: FHIP1B associated almost exclusively with punctate structures.
source: FHIP1B associated almost exclusively with punctate structures (Figure 4C, Video 1), while FHIP2A associated with both punctate and tubular structures (Figure 4D, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4C and Video 1.

claim: FHIP2A associated with both punctate and tubular structures.
source: FHIP1B associated almost exclusively with punctate structures (Figure 4C, Video 1), while FHIP2A associated with both punctate and tubular structures (Figure 4D, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4D and Video 1.

claim: FHIP1B colocalized with motile and nonmotile Rab5B early endosomes.
source: We found that FHIP1B colocalized with motile and nonmotile Rab5B early endosomes via live-cell imaging (Figure 5B, C, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5B, C, and Video 3.

claim: FHIP1B colocalized with Rab5A via immunofluorescence.
source: FHIP1B also colocalized with Rab5A via immunofluorescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of FHIP1B resulted in an accumulation of endosomes near the centrosome.
source: Furthermore, the overexpression of FHIP1B present in our FHIP1B KO lines expressing FHIP1B-TagRFPT resulted in an accumulation of endosomes near the centrosome (Figure 5D), suggesting that FHIP1B may link dynein to early endosomes, resulting in their transport to the minus ends of microtubules located near the centrosome.
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hook1 and Hook3 colocalized with Rab5B early endosomes.
source: Using spinning-disk confocal imaging, we found that Hook1 and Hook3 colocalized with Rab5B early endosomes, while Hook2 did not (Figure 5E, Videos 4–6, controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that an FHF complex containing FHIP1B and Hook1 or Hook3 links dynein to Rab5B early endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Videos 4–6.

claim: Hook2 did not colocalize with Rab5B early endosomes.
source: Using spinning-disk confocal imaging, we found that Hook1 and Hook3 colocalized with Rab5B early endosomes, while Hook2 did not (Figure 5E, Videos 4–6, controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that an FHF complex containing FHIP1B and Hook1 or Hook3 links dynein to Rab5B early endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Videos 4–6.

claim: GMPPNP-bound Rab5B bound FHIP1B to a higher extent as compared to GDP-bound Rab5B.
source: We found that GMPPNP-bound Rab5B bound FHIP1B to a higher extent as compared to GDP-bound Rab5B (Figure 5F), consistent with the hypothesis that FHIP1B binds to membrane-bound Rab5B.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: FHIP1B coimmunoprecipitated with Rab5B.
source: FHIP1B coimmunoprecipitated with Rab5B, as expected, but we did not detect an interaction with any of the 12 other Rab GTPases tested (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: FHIP1B did not coimmunoprecipitate with Rab1A, 2, 3A, 4A, 6A, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, or 18.
source: FHIP1B coimmunoprecipitated with Rab5B, as expected, but we did not detect an interaction with any of the 12 other Rab GTPases tested (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: FHIP2A colocalized with GMAP210, SCFD1, and BET1.
source: We found that FHIP2A colocalized with GMAP210, SCFD1, and BET1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), further confirming that FHIP2A is involved in ER-to-Golgi transport.
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FHIP2A strongly colocalized with GFP-Rab1A.
source: We found that FHIP2A strongly colocalized with GFP-Rab1A, which is crucial for several steps in ER-to-Golgi trafficking (Saraste et al., 1995; Tisdale et al., 1992; Westrate et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021), but none of the other small GTPases tested (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: FHIP2A did not colocalize with Rab2, Rab18, Arf1, or Sar1.
source: We found that FHIP2A strongly colocalized with GFP-Rab1A, which is crucial for several steps in ER-to-Golgi trafficking (Saraste et al., 1995; Tisdale et al., 1992; Westrate et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021), but none of the other small GTPases tested (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: FHIP2A did not immunoprecipitate with Rab1A.
source: However, FHIP2A did not immunoprecipitate with Rab1A or any of the other 12 Rabs (Rab2, 3A, 4A, 5B, 6A, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, and 18) we tested (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B), suggesting that this interaction may be indirect or require additional molecular interactions between FHIP2A and ER-to-Golgi transport intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by the coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Hook2 showed strong colocalization with Rab1A.
source: We found that Hook2 showed strong colocalization with Rab1A (Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Video 9.

claim: Hook3 showed some colocalization with Rab1A.
source: Hook3 also showed some colocalization with Rab1A (Video 10), while Hook1 showed very little colocalization with Rab1A (Figure 6D, Video 8, controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Video 10.

claim: Hook1 showed very little colocalization with Rab1A.
source: Hook3 also showed some colocalization with Rab1A (Video 10), while Hook1 showed very little colocalization with Rab1A (Figure 6D, Video 8, controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6D and Video 8.

claim: In cells expressing either wild-type or GTP-locked Rab1A, FHIP2A strongly colocalized with Rab1A tubules.
source: In cells expressing either wild-type or GTP-locked Rab1A, FHIP2A strongly colocalized with Rab1A tubules (Figure 7A, Video 11), and at least 73% of cells had more than five motile Rab1A and FHIP2A tubules (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7A and Video 11.

claim: At least 73% of cells expressing wild-type or GTP-locked Rab1A had more than five motile Rab1A and FHIP2A tubules.
source: In cells expressing either wild-type or GTP-locked Rab1A, FHIP2A strongly colocalized with Rab1A tubules (Figure 7A, Video 11), and at least 73% of cells had more than five motile Rab1A and FHIP2A tubules (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In cells expressing GDP-locked Rab1A, 0% of cells had more than five motile Rab1A tubules.
source: On the other hand, in cells expressing GDP-locked Rab1A (Figure 7A), 0% of cells had more than five motile Rab1A tubules, and only 22% of cells had more than five motile FHIP2A tubules (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In cells expressing GDP-locked Rab1A, only 22% of cells had more than five motile FHIP2A tubules.
source: On the other hand, in cells expressing GDP-locked Rab1A (Figure 7A), 0% of cells had more than five motile Rab1A tubules, and only 22% of cells had more than five motile FHIP2A tubules (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There was a 39% decrease in the number of motile Rab1A tubules in FHIP2A KO cells compared to control cells.
source: We found a 39% decrease in the number of motile Rab1A tubules in FHIP2A KO cells compared to control cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The number of motile Rab1A tubules was rescued in FHIP2A KO cells expressing FHIP2A-TagRFP-T.
source: The number of motile Rab1A tubules was rescued in FHIP2A KO cells expressing FHIP2A-TagRFP-T, suggesting that FHIP2A is involved in the formation and/or motility of Rab1A tubules.
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Tubule length was slightly, but significantly, decreased in FHIP2A KO cells compared to the rescue cells.
source: We found that tubule length was slightly, but significantly, decreased in FHIP2A KO cells compared to the rescue cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that FHIP2A likely plays a larger role in tubule motility rather than formation.
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The FHF complex has been implicated in linking dynein to cargo in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus nidulans and human cells.
source: The FHF complex has been implicated in linking dynein to cargo in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus nidulans and human cells (Bielska et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2016; Mattera et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Bielska et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2016; Mattera et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: A. nidulans has one FTS (FtsA), one Hook (HookA), and one FHIP (FhipA), which together link dynein to early endosomes.
source: A. nidulans has one FTS (FtsA), one Hook (HookA), and one FHIP (FhipA), which together link dynein to early endosomes (Yao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Yao et al., 2014).

claim: Both the A. nidulans HookA and FtsA proteins require FhipA to associate with early endosomes.
source: Both the A. nidulans HookA and FtsA proteins require FhipA to associate with early endosomes (Yao et al., 2014), suggesting that the FHIP protein mediates cargo recognition and binding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Yao et al., 2014).

claim: The initially described 'FHF' complex was identified by immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry (MS) of FTS in HeLa cells.
source: The initially described 'FHF' complex was identified by immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry (MS) of FTS in HeLa cells (Xu et al., 2008), and was found to contain FHIP1B, FTS, Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Xu et al., 2008).

claim: The initially described 'FHF' complex was found to contain FHIP1B, FTS, Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3.
source: The initially described 'FHF' complex was identified by immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry (MS) of FTS in HeLa cells (Xu et al., 2008), and was found to contain FHIP1B, FTS, Hook1, Hook2, and Hook3.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Xu et al., 2008).

claim: FHIP1A binds FTS.
source: Further studies confirmed a similar FHF complex composition (Guo et al., 2016) and found that FHIP1A binds FTS (Mattera et al., 2020), suggesting that it may also be an FHF complex component.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Mattera et al., 2020).

claim: FHIP2A and FHIP2B were identified in Hook1 and Hook3 proteomic datasets previously generated in the Reck-Peterson laboratory.
source: FHIP2A and FHIP2B were identified in Hook1 and Hook3 proteomic datasets previously generated in our laboratory (Redwine et al., 2017), suggesting they may also be FHF complex components.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Redwine et al., 2017).

claim: The FHF complex (FTS, Hook1/2/3, and FHIP1B) has been shown to associate with homotypic fusion and protein sorting (HOPS) complex components and may be involved in late endosome/lysosome clustering and epidermal growth factor trafficking.
source: This FHF complex has been shown to associate with homotypic fusion and protein sorting (HOPS) complex components and may be involved in late endosome/lysosome clustering and epidermal growth factor trafficking (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Xu et al., 2008).

claim: In rat hippocampal neurons, an FHF complex of similar composition has been demonstrated to bind Rab5A and is involved in the retrograde axonal transport of transferrin receptor.
source: In rat hippocampal neurons, an FHF complex of similar composition has been demonstrated to bind Rab5A and is involved in the retrograde axonal transport of transferrin receptor (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Guo et al., 2016).

claim: A similar FHF complex has been demonstrated to link dynein to the AP-4 adaptor complex.
source: Finally, a similar FHF complex has also been demonstrated to link dynein to the AP-4 adaptor complex (Mattera et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Mattera et al., 2020).

claim: Processive dynein motility requires the dynactin complex and a coiled-coil activating adaptor.
source: In many organisms, processive dynein motility requires the dynactin complex and a coiled-coil activating adaptor (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).

claim: There are ~20 known or candidate activating adaptors in human cells.
source: There are ~20 known or candidate activating adaptors in human cells, several of which have been implicated in linking dynein to different cargos (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Several activating adaptors have been implicated in linking dynein to different cargos.
source: There are ~20 known or candidate activating adaptors in human cells, several of which have been implicated in linking dynein to different cargos (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: How activating adaptors link dynein to its cargo is only known in a few cases.
source: However, how activating adaptors link dynein to its cargo is only known in a few cases (Hoogenraad et al., 2001; Matanis et al., 2002; Schlager et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Hoogenraad et al., 2001; Matanis et al., 2002; Schlager et al., 2010).

claim: Rab1A is crucial for several steps in ER-to-Golgi trafficking.
source: We found that FHIP2A strongly colocalized with GFP-Rab1A, which is crucial for several steps in ER-to-Golgi trafficking (Saraste et al., 1995; Tisdale et al., 1992; Westrate et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021), but none of the other small GTPases tested (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Saraste et al., 1995; Tisdale et al., 1992; Westrate et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021).

claim: Combinatorial assembly of different FTS–Hook–FHIP complexes is one mechanism dynein uses to achieve cargo specificity.
source: Our findings suggest that combinatorial assembly of different FTS–Hook–FHIP complexes is one mechanism dynein uses to achieve cargo specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different FHF complexes associate with distinct motile cargos.
source: Live-cell imaging and biochemical approaches show that different FHF complexes associate with distinct motile cargos.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complexes composed of FTS, FHIP1B, and Hook1/Hook3 colocalize with Rab5-tagged early endosomes via a direct interaction between FHIP1B and GTP-bound Rab5.
source: Complexes composed of FTS, FHIP1B, and Hook1/Hook3 colocalize with Rab5-tagged early endosomes via a direct interaction between FHIP1B and GTP-bound Rab5.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complexes composed of FTS, FHIP2A, and Hook2 colocalize with Rab1A-tagged ER-to-Golgi cargos.
source: In contrast, complexes composed of FTS, FHIP2A, and Hook2 colocalize with Rab1A-tagged ER-to-Golgi cargos and FHIP2A is involved in the motility of Rab1A tubules.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: FHIP2A is involved in the motility of Rab1A tubules.
source: In contrast, complexes composed of FTS, FHIP2A, and Hook2 colocalize with Rab1A-tagged ER-to-Golgi cargos and FHIP2A is involved in the motility of Rab1A tubules.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: FHIP1B is a Rab5-specific effector.
source: Taken together, these data show that FHIP1B is a Rab5-specific effector.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An FHF complex containing FHIP1B and Hook1 or Hook3 links dynein to Rab5B early endosomes.
source: Using spinning-disk confocal imaging, we found that Hook1 and Hook3 colocalized with Rab5B early endosomes, while Hook2 did not (Figure 5E, Videos 4–6, controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that an FHF complex containing FHIP1B and Hook1 or Hook3 links dynein to Rab5B early endosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An FHF complex containing FHIP2A and Hook2 links dynein to Rab1A-marked tubular ER-to-Golgi transport intermediates.
source: Together our findings suggest that FTS/Hook2/FHIP2A complexes link dynein/dynactin to Rab1A-marked tubular ER-to-Golgi transport intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FHIP2A likely plays a larger role in tubule motility rather than formation.
source: We found that tubule length was slightly, but significantly, decreased in FHIP2A KO cells compared to the rescue cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that FHIP2A likely plays a larger role in tubule motility rather than formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Rab1A-FHIP2A interaction is likely indirect or requires additional molecular interactions between FHIP2A and ER-to-Golgi transport intermediates.
source: However, FHIP2A did not immunoprecipitate with Rab1A or any of the other 12 Rabs (Rab2, 3A, 4A, 5B, 6A, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, and 18) we tested (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B), suggesting that this interaction may be indirect or require additional molecular interactions between FHIP2A and ER-to-Golgi transport intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FHIP1B may link dynein to early endosomes, resulting in their transport to the minus ends of microtubules located near the centrosome.
